about.title: About the product
about.text: A schedule service for universities and apps for students.

window.lead: A service where a university keeps its schedule, and apps where students and teachers see it. This is the product's new version: all three clients were written anew from 2 June 2026.

what.title: What it is
what.p1: At a university the schedule is made by the academic office. In Pora na paru it lives in one place, and its changes reach the iOS and Android apps, the widgets and the site at once. A group, a teacher and a room each have a schedule of their own.

now.title: What already works
now.p1: The schedule in a browser has been open since 16 October 2026: the week of any group, teacher or room by a link, nothing to install. The iOS and Android apps are in an alpha test: the iOS store build has reached testers through TestFlight since 27 September, the Android one through a closed test in Google Play since 30 September. Anyone can try them: the links are in these lessons' windows. The site poranaparu.com has been live since 30 September.
now.p2: The editor for universities is being designed: there the schedule will be made and published to every app with one button.

role.title: My part
role.p1: I am the co-founder and CEO. I design the interfaces in Figma and write all three clients myself: iOS in SwiftUI, Android in Jetpack Compose, the web in Next.js. The backend and the server are my co-founder's.

how.title: How the work goes
how.p1: Each client is a repository of its own with its own knowledge base: feature specs, a log of decisions and automatic checks. Decisions go into the log, so one sees not only how a thing was made but why.

origin.title: The start: VCourse
origin.text: The first version. Launched on 1 September 2025, 632 downloads in three days.

window.lead: The product's first version. On it the idea was tried by real users.

why.title: Where the idea came from
why.p1: Checking the schedule of my own lessons was awkward. Some universities had apps of their own for it, and from 2023 a classmate and I talked about one for ours, but kept putting it off: the idea seemed too big.

build.title: How we made it
build.p1: In our third year, in September 2024, we were given a semester for a product of our own idea. I took product design and the front end, my classmate the backend and DevOps. I had no experience in mobile development at all: the first semester went on Swift, SwiftUI, Xcode and Apple's guidelines.
build.p2: The next semester and the summer went on polishing. The app was rewritten from scratch several times.

launch.title: The launch
launch.p1: On 1 September 2025 a post came out in the university's Telegram channel, and strangers began to download the app. In the first three days: 632 downloads, 411 of them on 2 September.
launch.p2: Within a semester of the launch came Android and the site, and five more institutions joined. Then came the question of what would keep the product going: that is «The fork», on Tuesday.

fork.title: The fork
fork.text: Ads in the app or a service for universities. We chose the service.

window.lead: After VCourse launched we had to decide what would carry the product: ads in the students' app or a service for universities. We chose the service.

question.title: The question
question.p1: In the semester after the launch the Android app and the site came out and five more schools joined. The app was free and had no ads, and we could not develop it seriously while earning nothing from it.

ceiling.title: The app's ceiling
ceiling.p1: VCourse took the schedule from the universities' websites. Any redesign of such a site broke the schedule in the app, and the app gave the university itself nothing.
ceiling.p2: The only way to earn from it was ads. We did not want to put them in.

heard.title: What we heard
heard.p1: Students learn about changes from chats, from their group leads or once they are in the room: the official schedule does not show last-minute changes.
heard.p2: In an academic office the standard system cannot make a one-off replacement of a teacher: the lesson is cancelled and the dean's office phones the students. The interviews with students and academic offices were done by the team.

choice.title: What we chose
choice.p1: A service in which the academic office makes the schedule itself and publishes it to every app at once. The university becomes the source of the data, and the students' apps become part of the service.
choice.p2: VCourse has not been updated since February 2026. In April we pitched to investors at the Tramplin technopark with the service for universities, and on 2 June we started the new version, Pora na paru.

ios.title: The iOS app
ios.text: SwiftUI, a Live Activity and widgets. The build is in TestFlight.

window.lead: A native app in SwiftUI: the schedule, notes, widgets, Live Activity and Siri shortcuts. Since 27 September 2026 its store build has been with testers in TestFlight.

try.title: Try it
try.p1: The alpha is open by a link: TestFlight, Apple's app for betas, installs and updates it. It needs an iPhone with iOS 17 or later.

what.title: What it does
what.p1: The week of a group, a teacher or a room, subgroups, search across six directories and in Spotlight. A lesson can carry a note with photos and a reminder.
what.p2: The schedule is kept on the phone and opens offline: the Storage screen shows what is saved and how much room it takes.

outside.title: Outside the app
outside.p1: Live Activity keeps the current lesson on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island and moves on by itself from the lesson to the break and the end of the day. The server sends no updates yet, so the card carries its next phase in advance and switches to it by the schedule it already knows.
outside.p2: There are nine widgets: six on the lock screen and three on the home screen — notes that can be ticked off in the widget, favourites and a calendar of lessons. Plus eight Siri shortcuts and quick actions on the icon.

reminders.title: Reminders
reminders.p1: Notifications are set by rules rather than a bell on each lesson: reminders of notes, a morning and an evening summary of the day, and important lessons — office hours, tests and exams. The system allows an app 64 scheduled notifications; the app keeps its queue at 60.

how.title: How it is built
how.p1: Swift 6 and SwiftUI, iOS 17 and later, Liquid Glass on iOS 26. Six modules on Tuist, storage on SwiftData, and one outside dependency: a snapshot testing library.
how.p2: The store build and the internal one, with made-up data, are two different targets: the test data cannot reach the store even by mistake.

android.title: The Android app
android.text: Compose and Material 3 Expressive, the current lesson in a widget.

window.lead: A native app in Jetpack Compose with Material 3 Expressive. The alpha reaches testers through a closed test in Google Play.

try.title: Try it
try.p1: The alpha installs from Google Play and updates like any other app. The closed test is open to anyone who joins the testers' group. It needs a phone with Android 10 or later and Google Play.

what.title: What it does
what.p1: The same as on iOS, by Android's rules: the week of a group, a teacher or a room, subgroups, search across the directories, notes with photos and notifications. A building has its map.
what.p2: The schedule is kept on the phone and opens offline.

widgets.title: Widgets
widgets.p1: Four widgets on Glance: favourites, a calendar of lessons, notes that can be ticked off without opening the app, and a first version of the current lesson's widget. Android has no Live Activity, so a widget shows the current lesson: the system's timer counts the minutes, and the progress bar steps once a minute.

colour.title: Colour
colour.p1: Seventeen accents to choose from. From each one Material 3 builds a light and a dark scheme; all 34 schemes are exported from the generator in advance rather than computed on the phone.

how.title: How it is built
how.p1: Kotlin, Compose, Android 10 and later. Eleven Gradle modules, Hilt, Room and Navigation 3. In tests an interceptor of network requests stands in for the server, and the store build is checked for having no test data in it.
how.p2: The privacy check found seven permissions in the build instead of two: libraries had added five of them.

web.title: The schedule in a browser
web.text: The whole week by a link, nothing to install. Live since 16 October 2026.

window.lead: The week of any group, teacher or room by a link, nothing to install. Live since 16 October 2026.

what.title: What it does
what.p1: The week's grid by the university's bells: today is tinted, the current lesson has a ring and the time left, and a line shows the hour. The page opens already scrolled to the nearest lesson, and the weeks page years forward and back.
what.p2: Search on ⌘K looks through groups, teachers, rooms, faculties, departments and buildings. A lesson has its window, a room has its building's map, and subgroups switch by tabs.

time.title: The university's time
time.p1: “Now”, “today” and the time left are counted in the university's time zone: a student looking at the schedule from another city sees what the room sees.

how.title: How it is built
how.p1: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4 and shadcn/ui on Radix. The pages are rendered on the server and refreshed every five minutes, and only the server talks to the API.
how.p2: 17 automatic checks: accessibility to WCAG 2.2 AA in both themes, addresses, SEO and the JavaScript budget. The schedule screen is allowed 250 KB gzip; the week's grid weighed 196.6 KB on 18 October 2026.

phone.title: On a phone
phone.p1: For now it is a plain list of lessons by day. A full phone screen is ahead, and the pages stay closed to search engines until the schedule takes its final shape.

system.title: The design system
system.text: One set of tokens from Figma and lesson colours on every platform.

window.lead: One palette and one set of lesson type colours on iOS, on Android and in the web. Each platform has its own way of getting there.

one.title: A lesson's type is a colour
one.p1: A lecture, a practice or an exam is known by its colour on any screen: in a card, in a widget, in a lesson's window. In the light theme it is shade 500 of the Tailwind palette, in the dark one 300.

figma.title: From Figma to code
figma.p1: Figma's variables are exported as a snapshot in the W3C Design Tokens format: 527 tokens in 11 files. A script builds the web's CSS from the snapshot, with pairs for the light and the dark theme.
figma.p2: The Tokens check lets no commit through if the CSS has drifted from the snapshot: a colour is changed in Figma, not in the code.

platforms.title: Three platforms
platforms.p1: On iOS the same values are written in Swift. Android takes the shade as a seed: the Material 3 generator builds the roles for the light and the dark theme from it, and a check forbids colours and sizes in the code outside the design system's module.
platforms.p2: What the three clients share is the palette and the match of lesson type to shade. The rest each platform does by its own rules: HIG on iOS, Material 3 Expressive on Android.

here.title: On this page
here.p1: The week and the lesson windows here are built on the same values: the brand's blue, zinc greys, the type colours and the Geist typeface. The sizes are 1.25 times larger.

editor.title: The editor
editor.text: Catches conflicts before publishing. Still being designed.

window.lead: A workspace where the academic office will make the schedule and publish it to every app at once. It is being designed; there is no code yet.

what.title: What it will be
what.p1: The features for the release were named on 29 September 2026: the schedule editor, the directories, publishing to every app, notifications of changes, import and integrations, and roles.
what.p2: In the editor lessons are dragged, weeks are built from templates, and subgroups and replacements are part of the schedule. A room or a teacher booked for two lessons at once is highlighted before publishing.

pain.title: Where it starts
pain.p1: The first scenario is a methodologist replacing a teacher who is ill. Today the standard system cannot make such a replacement, and the design starts with it.

before.title: What VCourse taught
before.p1: I designed the first editor of this kind for VCourse. A conflict there was only a clash of resources: one teacher, room or group in two places at once. Subgroups studying side by side were not a conflict.
before.p2: Any edit could be undone, and publishing went in two steps: a summary of all the changes, a check on the server, and only then one transaction. A contradictory schedule could not be published. The server's check was my co-founder's.

now.title: Now
now.p1: The workspace will come after sign-in with an account. The scenarios' screens are being drawn in Figma.

launch.title: VCourse's launch
launch.p1: On 1 September 2025 a post came out in the university's Telegram channel. In the first three days there were 632 downloads, 411 of them on 2 September. By 4 October 2026 there were 3,428 downloads in the App Store.

code.title: The new version's code
code.p1: 2,642 commits in three clients over five months. iOS came first, Android started on 10 August and the web on 29 September, and the months show the work moving from one client to the next.

sources.title: Where the numbers come from
sources.p1: Downloads, impressions and the chart position come from App Store Connect's export. Commits come from git log in the clients' repositories, without Dependabot's. Tests, decisions and specs are counted from the repositories' files.
sources.p2: Usage numbers are published with my co-founder's consent. They are counted again before each publication.

cabinet.title: The university's workspace
